items: Saying "3 commits ahead" without a base. Root cause: ahead and behind are counted from a merge base with a second ref, and Git has no default "parent" to compare with.
Using two dots in git diff to see what a branch changed. Root cause: in git diff, A..B compares the tips directly; A...B compares from the merge base.
Asking Git which branch a branch was created from. Root cause: a branch stores one commit ID and no origin; the only trace is a local reflog line.
Reading "up to date with 'origin/main'" as the state of the server. Root cause: origin/main is the last-known state, updated only by fetch or push.
Feeding %(is-base:...) to automation. Root cause: it is a first-parent heuristic whose answer changes with the refs that exist.

beats.text: Here's a second puzzle. An engineer opens a review for a small change, one commit, on a branch they created from a colleague's feature branch. The review shows forty changed files. Their one commit is in there somewhere, under everything the colleague did. What went wrong? Say your guess out loud.
beats.tele: Here's a second puzzle. An engineer opens a review for a small change, one commit, on a branch they created from a colleague's feature branch. The review shows forty changed files. beats.text: Nothing is broken. The engineer assumed that Git knows which branch their branch was created from, and compares against that. Git doesn't know. Nothing in a repository records which branch a branch was created from. Every comparison needs a base that you name, and "3 commits ahead" is meaningless until you say ahead of what. Hold on to those forty files. They come back.

beats.text: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. A commit is one saved snapshot, and it points back at its parent. A branch is a name that points at one commit. You know what one branch is. This video is about the relation between two.

beats.text: Divergence and ancestry. In one sentence: two branches have diverged when neither tip is an ancestor of the other. Their merge base is the best common ancestor, and "ahead" and "behind" are counted from it. A tip is the commit a branch points at. An ancestor is any commit you reach by walking back through parents.
beats.tele: Divergence and ancestry. In one sentence: two branches have diverged when neither tip is an ancestor of the other. Their merge base is the best common ancestor, and "ahead" and "behind" are counted from it. A tip is the commit a branch points at. An ancestor is any commit you reach by walking back through parents.

beats.text: Precisely. A common ancestor is a commit reachable from both tips. The manual says: "One common ancestor is better than another common ancestor if the latter is an ancestor of the former", and a best one is a merge base. There can be more than one, which the videos on merge take up.
beats.tele: Precisely. A common ancestor is a commit reachable from both tips. The manual says: "One common ancestor is better than another common ancestor if the latter is an ancestor of the former", and a best one is a merge base. There can be more than one, which the videos on merge take up.

beats.text: Ranges are sets of commits. A..B, two dots, is everything reachable from B but not from A. A...B, three dots, is the symmetric difference: reachable from one side but not both. git merge-base --is-ancestor A B exits with 0 when A is an ancestor of B, and with 1 when it is not.
beats.tele: Ranges are sets of commits. `A..B`, two dots, is everything reachable from B but not from A. `A...B`, three dots, is the symmetric difference: reachable from one side but not both. `git merge-base --is-ancestor A B` exits with 0 when A is an ancestor of B, and with 1 when it is not.

beats.text: The dots mean something else in git diff. This is a known trap, and the textbook gives it a table. Almost everyone falls into it once.
beats.tele: The dots mean something else in `git diff`. This is a known trap, and the textbook gives it a table. Almost everyone falls into it once.

beats.text: Read the table one column at a time. In git log and git rev-list, A..B is the commits reachable from B and not from A, and A...B is the commits reachable from exactly one side. In git diff, A..B compares the two tips directly, the same as git diff A B. And A...B compares from the merge base of A and B to B: what B changed.
beats.tele: Read the table one column at a time. In `git log` and `git rev-list`, `A..B` is the commits reachable from B and not from A, and `A...B` is the commits reachable from exactly one side. In `git diff`, `A..B` compares the two tips directly, the same as `git diff A B`. And `A...B` compares from the merge base of A and B to B: what B changed.

beats.text: No parent branch. In one sentence: nothing in a repository records which branch a branch was created from. The only trace is a line in a local reflog, and every comparison needs a base that you name. Look at the picture: three branch names on one line of commits, and nothing says which came from which.
beats.tele: No parent branch. In one sentence: nothing in a repository records which branch a branch was created from. The only trace is a line in a local reflog, and every comparison needs a base that you name. Look at the picture: three branch names on one line of commits, and nothing says which came from which.

beats.text: Look for the relationship in each place it could be. The new ref holds an ID. The commit it names has no field for a branch. The local configuration has no entry for it. The only mention is the reflog line branch: Created from the other branch. The reflog is a local journal of where a name has pointed. So that line exists in this clone and nowhere else, and git branch -D or reflog expiry removes it.
beats.tele: Look for the relationship in each place it could be. The new ref holds an ID. The commit it names has no field for a branch. The local configuration has no entry for it. The only mention is the reflog line `branch: Created from` the other branch. The reflog is a local journal of where a name has pointed. So that line exists in this clone and nowhere else, and `git branch -D` or reflog expiry removes it.

beats.text: git branch --contains answers "which branches reach this commit". That's reachability, not origin.
beats.tele: `git branch --contains` answers "which branches reach this commit". That's reachability, not origin.

beats.text: The nearest thing to an answer is a guess. The field %(is-base:<commit>) of git for-each-ref marks, in the manual's words, "the ref that is most likely the ref used as a starting point for the branch that produced" the commit. It's chosen by a first-parent heuristic, and the guess changes with the refs that exist. It exists since Git 2.47, and the textbook's recommendation is: a hint for humans, never an input to automation.

It's chosen by a first-parent heuristic, and the guess changes with the refs that exist. It exists since Git 2.47, and the textbook's recommendation is: a hint for humans, never an input to automation.

beats.text: One note on the platform side. A pull request has a base branch, chosen when it's opened, and it's stored by GitHub, not by Git. It's the one place where "created from" is recorded.

beats.text: Remote-tracking branches and upstream. In one sentence: a remote-tracking branch such as origin/main is a ref in your own repository that records the last position of a branch in another repository, and an upstream is two configuration lines that pair a local branch with one.
beats.tele: Remote-tracking branches and upstream. In one sentence: a remote-tracking branch such as `origin/main` is a ref in your own repository that records the last position of a branch in another repository, and an upstream is two configuration lines that pair a local branch with one.

beats.text: Remote-tracking branches live under refs/remotes/<remote>/. When a teammate pushes, your origin/main stays where it was, until git fetch updates it.
beats.tele: Remote-tracking branches live under `refs/remotes/<remote>/`. When a teammate pushes, your `origin/main` stays where it was, until `git fetch` updates it.

beats.text: The upstream of a branch B is configured by branch.B.remote and branch.B.merge, and B@{upstream}, or @{u}, names the corresponding remote-tracking branch. git status -sb and git branch -v compare a branch with its upstream. Nothing in that comparison talks to the server.
beats.tele: The upstream of a branch B is configured by `branch.B.remote` and `branch.B.merge`, and `B@{upstream}`, or `@{u}`, names the corresponding remote-tracking branch. `git status -sb` and `git branch -v` compare a branch with its upstream. Nothing in that comparison talks to the server.

beats.text: A branch created from another local branch has no upstream. A branch created from a remote-tracking branch gets one automatically, by branch.autoSetupMerge, which defaults to true.
beats.tele: A branch created from another local branch has no upstream. A branch created from a remote-tracking branch gets one automatically, by `branch.autoSetupMerge`, which defaults to `true`.

beats.text: When this arithmetic is the wrong tool. When the question is about content and not commits. A squash merge puts a branch's content into main without any of its commits, and then the ranges say "three commits ahead" about work that has landed. The next video deals with that blind spot.

beats.text: Picture a road that forks. Two cars start at the fork and drive down different arms. The fork is the merge base. "Ahead by three" is how far one car has driven from the fork, and "behind by two" is how far the other has.
beats.tele: Picture a road that forks. Two cars start at the fork and drive down different arms. The fork is the merge base. "Ahead by three" is how far one car has driven from the fork, and "behind by two" is how far the other has.

beats.text: Now the limit of the picture, which is the point of the video. On a real road, each arm has a name painted on a sign at the fork, so you know which arm branched off which. In Git there is no sign. The fork is a commit, and both arms are equally "the road". Which one you call the trunk is your decision, made each time you compare.

In Git there is no sign. The fork is a commit, and both arms are equally "the road". Which one you call the trunk is your decision, made each time you compare.

beats.text: And for remote-tracking branches: origin/main is a photograph of where the other car was when you last looked. Until you look again, with a fetch, every "ahead" and "behind" is measured against the photograph.

beats.tele: A branch created from another local branch has no upstream. A branch created from a remote-tracking branch gets one automatically, which is what the line `set up to track` reports.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: Saying "3 commits ahead" without a base. Root cause: ahead and behind are counted from a merge base with a second ref, and Git has no default "parent" to compare with.
beats.tele: Saying "3 commits ahead" without a base. Root cause: ahead and behind are counted from a merge base with a second ref, and Git has no default "parent" to compare with.

beats.text: Using two dots in git diff to see what a branch changed. Root cause: in git diff, A..B compares the tips directly; A...B compares from the merge base.
beats.tele: Using two dots in `git diff` to see what a branch changed. Root cause: in `git diff`, `A..B` compares the tips directly; `A...B` compares from the merge base.

beats.text: Asking Git which branch a branch was created from. Root cause: a branch stores one commit ID and no origin; the only trace is a local reflog line.
beats.tele: Asking Git which branch a branch was created from. Root cause: a branch stores one commit ID and no origin; the only trace is a local reflog line.

beats.text: Reading "up to date with 'origin/main'" as the state of the server. Root cause: origin/main is the last-known state, updated only by fetch or push.
beats.tele: Reading "up to date with 'origin/main'" as the state of the server. Root cause: `origin/main` is the last-known state, updated only by fetch or push.

beats.text: Feeding %(is-base:...) to automation. Root cause: it is a first-parent heuristic whose answer changes with the refs that exist.
beats.tele: Feeding `%(is-base:...)` to automation. Root cause: it is a first-parent heuristic whose answer changes with the refs that exist.

beats.text: Now, out of the lab. Stacked branches are where this bites, as the textbook describes. Branch B was created from branch A. A is merged with a squash, or deleted. B's "changes against main" suddenly include everything A did, because the base you implied no longer exists. That's the forty-file review from the hook. The repair is git rebase --onto, which moves B to its real base. The rebase videos cover it.

The repair is `git rebase --onto`, which moves B to its real base. The rebase videos cover it.

beats.text: And the general rule for reports and dashboards. [ahead 2, behind 3] in git status, the counts on a pull request, "can this be fast-forwarded", and "which commits does this release contain" are all this arithmetic. Compute them with ranges, not with dates, and state the base.

beats.text: Answer out loud. A strong answer goes through the places where such a fact could be stored, and says what each holds. It names the local trace and the heuristic, with the limits of both. Then it separates the layers: what Git stores, and what the platform stores.
